# Notation and conventions {#sec-conventions}

This page fixes the notation of the whole tutorial. The tables are shared with the other tutorials of the site, so a
symbol means the same thing here as in [Fundamentals of Mathematics for Physicists](../../fundamentals-of-mathematics-for-physicists/index.qmd)
and [Fundamentals of Theoretical Physics](../../fundamentals-of-theoretical-physics/index.qmd). The chapters follow this
notation, including the metric signature and the other sign and normalisation conventions, whatever notation their
sources use; where a chapter quotes a source's convention, it says so and names the source. The last section lists
what is particular to Kaluza-Klein theories: the higher-dimensional fields, the internal coordinates and the internal
metric.

## Who these lectures are for

The reader is assumed to know calculus of one and several variables and linear algebra at the level of a first
university course, and to have met Newtonian mechanics. Nothing else is assumed: the foundations of mathematics
(Part I) develop set theory and topology, linear algebra, real and complex analysis, differential equations, Fourier
analysis, Hilbert spaces and operator theory, probability, differential geometry, Lie groups and their
representations, coset spaces and fibre bundles on explicit examples, and the foundations of physics (Part II)
develop, in this order, classical mechanics, classical electromagnetism, thermodynamics and statistical mechanics,
quantum mechanics, classical field theory, the Dirac equation, quantum field theory, gauge theories and symmetry
breaking, renormalisation, special and general relativity, supersymmetry and supergravity, each from its definitions. A reader who knows a chapter can skim its definitions and try its exercises.

## Reading the blocks {#sec-conventions-blocks}

Every numbered block of the book is one of three kinds, told apart by the colour of its title. **Statements**, that
is, definitions, theorems, lemmas, propositions and corollaries, have a red title and stand in a light red box; each definition introduces exactly one notion. **Examples**
have a green title; every statement is followed by a run of them, of increasing complexity, which carry the figures
and their interactive versions. **Exercises** have a blue title; every statement is followed by a run of them, of
increasing difficulty, each with a folded solution, and every chapter ends with exercises that draw on all of its
sections. To keep the line of the argument visible, the examples of a statement are folded into one collapsed
**Examples** box placed right after it, and its exercises, with their solutions, into one collapsed **Exercises**
box; open them to work through the material. Solutions that compute show the code and its output.

## Connection and curvature {#sec-conventions-curvature}

{{< include ../../_notation/curvature-gravity.qmd >}}

The chapters cite the two defining formulas by number. The Christoffel symbols of the Levi-Civita connection are
$$
\Gamma^k_{ij} = \tfrac12 g^{kl} \left( \partial_i g_{lj} + \partial_j g_{li} - \partial_l g_{ij} \right),
$$ {#eq-christoffel-def}
[@plebanski2024introduction, eq. 7.12; @carroll1997, eq. 3.21]
and the Riemann tensor is
$$
R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu \Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} - \partial_\nu \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma}
  + \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\lambda} \Gamma^\lambda_{\nu\sigma} - \Gamma^\rho_{\nu\lambda} \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\sigma}.
$$ {#eq-riemann-def}
[@plebanski2024introduction, eq. 6.4; @carroll1997, eq. 3.67].

## Conventions specific to this tutorial

Spacetime $M_4$ has coordinates $x^\mu$. Internal (compact) coordinates are $y^m$, and the full higher-dimensional
coordinates are $z^M = (x^\mu, y^m)$. Internal metrics are **negative definite**, so that the full metric
$\hat g_{MN}$ has signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$: the Kaluza-Klein ansatz reads $d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu -
\phi^2(dy + A_\mu dx^\mu)^2$ on a circle of radius $r$, with $y \sim y + 2\pi r$, and
$g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ on a sphere of radius $r$. We write
$h_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$ for the internal block, with $\gamma_{mn}$ the positive-definite metric used when the internal
geometry is discussed on its own (Riemannian metrics are positive definite). Under the circle ansatz the
higher-dimensional curvature scalar is $\hat R = R + \tfrac14\phi^2 F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} - 2\phi^{-1}\Box\phi$
[@plebanski2024introduction, eq. 13.24].

The Kaluza-Klein literature is split on the signature: @overduin1998 [Sec. 3], @tanii1998 [Sec. 2] and the CSDR reviews
[@manolakos2016, eq. 9; @manousselis2000, Sec. 2] use $(+,-,-,-)$ as we do, while @duff1994 [p. 2], @duff2025 [p. 3]
and @martin1997 [eq. 2.3] use $(-,+,+,+)$. Where we quote a formula from a source with the other signature, we say so and convert
with the rule of the geometry table above.

The anti-Hermitian generators are the convention of the CSDR literature
[@kubyshin2003, p. 10; @chatzistavrakidis2007consistency, eq. 2.4], in which the generators of a coset $S/R$ are split into $Q_i$ spanning
$\mathfrak r$ and $Q_a$ spanning its complement $\mathfrak k$. @manolakos2016 [eq. 1] and @manousselis2000 [eqs. 4, 6] write
$F_{MN} = \partial_M A_N - \partial_N A_M - [A_M, A_N]$ with $D_M = \partial_M - A_M$, which is the same convention after
$A \to -A$; @kubyshin2003 [eqs. 9, 36] prints the commutator with a minus sign in his eq. (9) but uses $F = dA + A\wedge A$ in his
example (see the reading note). We never need a gauge coupling inside the internal space, since CSDR fixes the
internal components of $A$ in units of the coset radius.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\hat g_{MN}$, $\hat R$, $\hat A_M$, $\hat F_{MN}$, $\hat S$ | a hat marks a higher-dimensional quantity: metric, curvature scalar, gauge field, field strength, action |
| $\hat\kappa$, $\hat G$ | higher-dimensional gravitational coupling and Newton constant, $\hat\kappa^2 = 8\pi\hat G$; a subscript ($G_5$, $\kappa_5$) is used only when the dimension must be named |
| $y^m$, $m = 1, \dots, n$ | internal coordinates; $y$ on the circle |
| $z^M = (x^\mu, y^m)$ | higher-dimensional coordinates; $M$, $N$ curved higher-dimensional indices |
| $a$, $b$ | flat (frame) indices in four dimensions |
| $A$, $B$ | flat indices in $4 + n$ dimensions, and labels of the generators of $S$ |
| $M_4$ | four-dimensional spacetime |
| $X$ | internal manifold of dimension $n$ ($S/R$ when it is a coset) |
| $\gamma_{mn}$ | positive-definite internal metric |
| $h_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$ | internal block of $\hat g_{MN}$, negative definite |
| $R_\gamma$ | curvature scalar of the internal metric $\gamma$ |
| $r$ | radius of the internal circle or sphere; the circle has $y \sim y + 2\pi r$ |
| $\phi$ | Kaluza-Klein scalar; the circle has circumference $2\pi r\phi$ |
| $\sigma = \sqrt3\log\phi$ | dilaton |
| $\Omega$ | Weyl factor, $\tilde g = \Omega^2 g$ (in the compactification survey, the holomorphic $(m, 0)$-form) |
| $g^E_{\mu\nu}$ | Einstein-frame metric |
| $\omega_{\mathrm{BD}}$ | Brans-Dicke parameter |
| $K_a = K_a{}^m\partial_m$ | Killing vectors of the internal metric |
| $c_{ab}{}^c$ | structure constants of the Killing vectors, $[K_a, K_b] = c_{ab}{}^c K_c$; on the sphere $c_{ab}{}^c = -\epsilon_{abc} = -f_{ab}{}^c$, opposite to the gauge algebra |
| $\xi^M$ | generator of a diffeomorphism |
| $\Phi(x, y)$, $\Phi_n(x)$ | higher-dimensional field and its Kaluza-Klein modes, $\Phi = \sum_n \Phi_n(x)\,e^{iny/r}$ with $\Phi_n = \frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_0^{2\pi r}\Phi\,e^{-iny/r}\,dy$ |
| $m_n = \lvert n\rvert/r$ | mass of the mode $n$ |
| $q_n$ | charge of the mode $n$, proportional to $n/r$, with the sign fixed by $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + iqA_\mu$ |
| $\langle\cdot\rangle$ | average over the internal space |
| $\operatorname{Vol}(X)$ | volume of the internal manifold |
| $R$ | in the coset chapters, the isotropy group of $S/R$; it never appears in a formula with the scalar curvature |
| $Q_i$, $Q_a$ | generators spanning $\mathfrak r$ and $\mathfrak k$ |
| $\phi_a$ | CSDR scalars, the internal components of $\hat A$ |
| $\tau: R \to G$ | CSDR embedding of the isotropy group in the gauge group |
| $H = C_G(\tau(R))$ | four-dimensional gauge group, the centraliser of $\tau(R)$ |
| $\theta_W$ | Weinberg angle |
| $\mathcal N$ | number of supersymmetries (the normal distribution never appears in this tutorial) |
| $h^{p,q}$, $\chi$ | Hodge numbers, Euler number |
| $J$ | Kähler form |
| $\mathcal G_{ab}$ | gauge coupling matrix of a reduction on $X$, the average of $K_a\cdot K_b$ over $X$; the reduced action contains $-\tfrac14\mathcal G_{ab}F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{b\,\mu\nu}$ |
| $\mu$ | Scherk-Schwarz twist mass parameter, with monodromy $e^{2\pi i\mu r}$ around the circle |
| $\rho_F$ | representation of $G$ carried by the higher-dimensional fermions in CSDR |
| $\Lambda_{1/2}(s, y)$ | lift of the isometry $s$ of $S/R$ to the spinors |
| $L$ | size of large extra dimensions, internal volume $L^n$ (the Arkani-Hamed-Dimopoulos-Dvali scenario) |
| $K_{abc}$ | contorsion (three frame indices; the Killing vectors $K_a$ carry one) |
| $\mathcal M$ | moduli space of a compactification; in the section on cosets with torsion, the geometric mass operator of the fermions |

- **Units:** $\hbar = c = 1$ throughout; Newton's constant is kept explicit through $\kappa^2 = 8\pi G_N$.
- **Hats:** in this tutorial a hat marks a higher-dimensional quantity, never a Fourier transform; Fourier modes on the
  circle are written $\Phi_n$.
- **Hermitian generators** appear only where the Standard Model or the fuzzy sphere is compared, and are then written
  $t_a = iT_a$.
- **Charges of the modes:** with the ansatz $dy + A_\mu dx^\mu$ and $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + iqA_\mu$, the mode
  $e^{iny/r}$ has charge $q_n = -n/r$ [@cecotti2023introduction, eq. (6.19)], that is $q_n = -ne$ with $e = \sqrt2\kappa/r$ [@duff1994, eq. 16].
